script: Devanagari, as observed in the canonical MorphoVerse dataset (Dogri's standard modern script; historically also written in the Takri script)
romanization_guidance: Represent aspirated and retroflex consonants with familiar reader-friendly digraphs rather than diacritics, matching the same reader-friendly convention used for other Devanagari-script languages in this corpus.
Use a widely-recognized conventional spelling for well-known names/places when one already exists in common English usage.
Keep every repeated occurrence of the same source term romanized identically within one poem.
linguistic_guidance: Dogri is closely related to, but distinct from, Punjabi and Hindi/Pahari varieties; shared vocabulary with Punjabi or Hindi is not evidence the poem's cultural content belongs to Punjabi or Hindi culture.
Dogri is spoken primarily in the Jammu region; do not conflate its grammar or vocabulary with generic Hindi or Punjabi without textual grounds -- assess each poem on its own terms.
cultural_boundary_rules: A culturally specific Dogri annotation requires a defensible link to a named tradition, practice, or symbol that the poem's own text actually evidences -- do not add one merely because the poem is in Dogri.

Distinguish Dogra/Jammu regional context from generic Punjabi Sikh culture and from generic Kashmiri culture, both of which border the Dogri-speaking region -- do not default to either without textual evidence.
Do not infer Dogra Rajput historical/courtly imagery, Jammu temple imagery, or Duggar folk-festival imagery unless the poem's own words name or unambiguously depict that specific content.
literary_context_cautions: Dogri has both an older courtly/devotional literary tradition and a modern post-1950s literary revival (Dogri gained official recognition as a Scheduled Language in 2003) -- do not assume a poem belongs to a specific era or tradition without textual evidence.
translation_cautions: Watch for postposition-carried case/relational meaning being flattened into a generic English preposition, similar to the caution already documented for Hindi.
Watch for regionally specific vocabulary shared with Punjabi/Pahari varieties being glossed with an over-general Hindi equivalent that loses a Dogri-specific nuance.
figurative_language_cautions: Repeated words or phrases used for rhythmic or emphatic effect are ordinary poetic technique in this region's literary tradition, not automatically a distinct figurative expression on each occurrence.
visual_representation_cautions: Do not default to Dogra-courtly, Jammu-temple, or generic Kashmiri/Punjabi imagery for a Dogri cultural entity unless the text specifically supports it.
negative_confusions for an entity in this language should name a plausible, specific incorrect substitution, not a generic stereotype disconnected from the poem's own evidence.
stereotype_avoidance_rules: Do not adopt a 'this is basically Punjabi' or 'this is basically Kashmiri' framing when annotating -- annotate only what this specific poem's text supports, as Dogri in its own right.
Do not apply a numeric quota (e.g. 'expect N cultural entities') to this poem -- a poem with zero text-supported cultural entities is a valid, expected outcome.
ambiguity_handling_rules: When a term could plausibly belong to shared Dogri/Punjabi/Pahari vocabulary and the text does not disambiguate its cultural role, prefer the conservative (non-cultural) reading.
When a reading is genuinely uncertain from the text alone, prefer the more conservative reading and use the explicit-uncertainty mechanism rather than asserting one interpretation as fact.
prohibited_assumptions: Do not assume Dogri content is interchangeable with Punjabi or Kashmiri content merely due to regional proximity.
Do not assume the speaker's religion, region, or gender beyond what the text states.
Do not assume a specific historical period unless the text itself places the poem there.
Do not assume rural versus urban setting unless the text specifies it.
